h.strategy: Most obvious hypotheses follow a local story: an option matters more when its substitute is missing. These are usually rated likely and often fail. Instead, base hypotheses on robust statistical regularities. (1) Headroom: helpful edits help less in parents that are already strong, for example parents that already contain the strongest option elsewhere. (2) Harmful edits hurt more in strong parents and look harmless in weak parents, because of floor effects. (3) Saturation: adding a second copy of a strong option gives smaller gains than adding the first. (4) Removing an option costs less when the parent has several similar options. Choose conditions that many parents satisfy, so the effect is detectable. Cover several edited fields and both directions. In each 'why', state the obvious prediction and the reason the opposite should hold.

hyps.why: Obvious: skip to the output is beneficial; but a second skip into the output node saturates.
Obvious: skip helps trainability; but when edge 3 already provides an identity path the added skip contributes less.
Obvious: removing the first edge cuts the network; but a strong parallel path from the input into node 2 provides redundancy.
Obvious: removal hurts more when fewer paths remain; but a parent already weak (edge 5 none) is near the accuracy floor, so removal looks harmless.
Obvious: dropping edges in a sparse parent is catastrophic; but floor effects make the additional loss small in an already-weak cell.
Obvious: edge 2 is minor, so edits matter little; but a strong parent exposes the weak-op penalty while weak parents mask it.
Obvious: more convs help; but a second conv1x1 into the output node saturates the benefit of the first.
Obvious: an extra conv helps independently; but with conv3x3 already on the parallel path to node 2, the second copy shows diminishing returns.
Obvious: conv3x3 on the first edge helps; but a parent already strong downstream from node 1 gains less (headroom).
Obvious: conv3x3 adds capacity everywhere; but a parent with a strong direct edge to the output leaves less headroom.
